speechtext: You have some job on your hands.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
Yes, but I like hard
jobs, I have come back with all my youth, and besides I notice that when you match your wits with one who will not agree with you, if you do not help him you help yourself. I hope it will not be considered as a breach of the etiquette of this aristocratic parliament of Canada (that an independent member should try to have a talk once in a while with a socialistic member like my hon. friend close to me, or a good Tory like the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White), or with a broad-minded Conservative such as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). I am happy to have a talk with the ministers of the crown, and I think this habit should be developed. It is another British precedent that ought to be copied and adopted in Canada, as it has been adopted in England. In that country they fight each other but respect each other as gentlemen and talk to each other. If hon. gentlemen will read the biographies of the Englishmen of the last century they will find that although they had battles and fierce struggles, even struggles between parties and nations-if you consider the Irish question- they still exchanged views and talked to each other quite freely. Gladstone had frequent conversations with Lord Salisbury. One day Lord Randolph Churchill, coming from dinner with Mr. Gladstone, turned to an old Liberal-Unionist and said' to him "What I cannot understand is why you should ever have abandoned the Old Man. Were I not a Tory, I could not be against him." Thus they have exchanges of amenities. I propose to play my humble part and to act as an independent member, to vote for the measures as they come up after I have heard the explanations of them, with entire disregard of the party interests of any group, but being careful not to cast a vote in a haphazard manner. Now if that idea were developed, could we not
[Mr. Bourassa.j
adapt the government situation to the parliamentary situation and have an understanding similar to that which Ramsay MacDonald had with the leaders of the two other parties, namely, that the government should take the House more into their confidence; that it should have less ministers and that the cabinet should be less autocratic and secret about its polices; that the ministers should not assume that they incorporate the whole wisdom of the country; that they should consult with and respect the feelings of the various members of the House, even members of the opposition; that the right of initiation of legislation, vested by the most venerable of British traditions in the individual members, should be more respected than it is in Canada and in England at present. On the other hand if the government is forced by circumstances to respect parliament more than past cabinets have, it seems to me that, as a matter of course, not of courtesy, parliament should also give a freer hand to the cabinet; that no government should be obliged to resign on a snap vote, because this evening or the other evening three members of parliament happen to be absent or other members of parliament could not agree to a certain action. I do not think a government should be defeated and compelled to resign and force an election simply because a minister may be defeated on a certain day at the hands of the majority, or that the government should resign because that item or this item should be reduced by the House.
I sum up the whole situation when I say that we must have greater liberty of expression of opinion in the House and greater liberty on the part of the government to administer affairs, but to administer them under the supervision and authority of the House of Commons. If this is not British policy, I ask my hon. friend for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to find the book, the page, the reference, the date and show me the precedent. But in the meantime I stick to my view.
In closing this long and rambling talk I apologize to my hon. friends on both sides of the House for having wearied them, but they must make allowance for my silence of eighteen years.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset let me express the pleasure which I have no doubt we feel in all quarters of this House that we have back with us an hon. member so well equipped intellectually and so well informed on all matters pertaining to this country, the empire and the world in general, as is the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I can well

Government's Right to Office
remember twenty-five years ago when I had the first opportunity of hearing the hon. member for Labelle in the House of Commons as it existed at that time. I well remember the important and distinguished position which the hon. member held in that House in the estimation of hon. members on both sides, and if I mention it without any disrespect or discourtesy -in those early days he was Jooked upon in parliament as a sort of theorist, an idealist, a visionary, I think I can say at this distance of time that he continues to bear some of the characteristics which we noticed then. If there be anything wanting in his wonderful mental equipment it is a touch of the practical, and that is what is most needed on the part of hon. members in this Chamber. The matters which we have to deal with, the questions which we have to consider, are questions of a very practical nature, and while we can enjoy and appreciate a discoursive address-a very academic address, I might call it-such as we have had this afternoon, still some of us are inclined to think that on a question such as that which is now before the House a few more practical suggestions from the hon. member for Labelle would have been much more to the purpose than the delightful discourse which he has given to the House this afternoon on almost every subject under the sun. He has, of his own choice, for many years, occupied a position of isolation in the public and political life of Canada. He is a man strong in his views and opinions, not easily moved by the views of others, a man not inclined to follow leadership, nor to confer, to discuss or to reason with others, but very largely influenced by his own mind in all matters. That is, perhaps, the reason of his isolation. There have been times when his hand has been against every man, and there have been other times when the hand of every man seemed to have been against him. Yet, with all his peculiarities and defects- and we all have defects, we must admit- we are glad to welcome him back in this Chamber. He is a very able debater, a well equipped parliamentarian, and by virtue of his great gift of oratory, clear reasoning power and ja discriminating taste in the use of language sets an example that we might with profit strive to emulate. We welcome him back, and if I say nothing further in regard to his effort this afternon, the reason is that I desire to confine my brief remarks to the question now before the House.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as leader of the government-and in speaking of the government in this debate I use the term
"government'' as one of convenience; I do not use it by way of admission that we have to-day a legally constituted government in this country-but as leader of the government for the time being he opened the debate by asking for the calm, moderate judgment of the House of Commons upon the question which is now the subject of debate in this House. I have no fault to find with the method iu which the Minister of Justice presented his side of the case. Anyone who watched him could see at once that he was labouring under a good deal of strain, suspense and excitement. But for the most part he managed to suppress his excitement and he delivered a fairly well balanced and well reasoned argument on the question before the House. The most notable point in his speech was his evasion or omission to discuss the most vital question in the amendment. He absolutely omitted to mention what we all consider to be the vital question and what the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), in his address last night, mentioned as the vital question, the real question, that is, the absence of the Prime Minister from a seat in this parliament. That, in my humble judgment, is the crux of the Whole matter.
I should like to deal for a few minutes with the effort of the Solicitor General in this debate; [DOT]but before doing so, may I say that one could hardly describe that effort as a judicial presentation of the government's case by one of the leading law officers of the crown. If wre are asked to give an unbiased, unprejudiced, impartial judgment upon the question now before us, the speech delivered last night by the Solicitor General could not be called a judicial presentation of the case. It was biased and it was prejudiced, full of inaccuracies, charged with exaggerations, with precedents not well chosen, not well digested and not quite fairly explained to the House of Commons. On the whole, however, I have no great objection to taking the speech as he made it last night. I believe with time he will improve. It Was his first effort in this House as Solicitor General of this country. As his first effort we should view it with charity and compliment him upon it, but it was by no means a judicial presentation of the government's case. It was such a (presentation of a case as one would expect to hear on the hustings or in some rough and tumble political meeting during an election.
We have been asked, as I said, to treat this question seriously, earnestly. If this government so intends us to treat this question, the government itself has made a very bad start. The start was made when the Speech from the

Government's Right to Office
Throne was prepared. That speech was a deliberate attempt on the part of the government to prejudice the question in the first instance. The Speech from the Throne is little short of a preelection manifesto, full of allurements, inducements, blandishments, to wave before the eyes of the Progressive and Independent members of this House. On Friday last we were ushered into the Senate chamber to hear it and on returning to this chamber, while the music of the speech was still jingling in the ears of Progressive members, we were treated to a decided innovation in this House. Instead of the usual motion to consider that Address, the traditional time-honoured motion, the leader of the government for the time being sought to steal a march on the House, and by a rather cheap artifice to introduce a novel measure, a motion of confidence in his own government. I wonder if in our search for precedents any precedent can be found of a government that has met parliament with a motion asking confidence in itself. I do not say that it is unprecedented, but I do say that it is most unusual; and during the course of twenty-five years at least I can say that it has never happened before in the parliament of Canada. The ordinary and well-established course which the government should have followed, was to meet the House, as they did, bring in the Address, as they did, and move for the consideration of that Address on a fixed day. That we expected; that we anticipated. Then the Address would have been proceeded with on that day so fixed, just as my hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) expected the government to do. This method would have given the House the usual opportunity of discussing the Address, and it would have given the opposition the opportunity which has always been afforded of moving any amendment they might see fit to propose. It is said, and it has been said to me by some Progressive members, 'Why did you not wait for the discussion of the Address?" We did not wait because the government tried to trick us in the matter; it tried to steal a march on us; it tried to spring a motion which it had no right to make inasmuch as such a motion must be preceded by notice. Then having defeated them in their object we could take no chances as to the government's next move. So on the first opportunity which offered, my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) moved the present amendment. Under the circumstances I say that he was absolutely right in doing so. I quite agree with the hon. member for Kindersley that this discussion might better have taken place on the discussion of the 
Speech from the Throne, and it would have taken place on that occasion had the government not attempted to trick us out of our opportunity.
The Speech from the Throne was prepared, as I say, as a sort of pre-election manifesto for the distinct purpose of swaying the Progressive and Independent vote in this parliament. It was the bait offered to the Progressives, and the motion of confidence which was to go before it was the hook: if they took the bait they must swallow the hook first. That is the position the government took; it was out fishing for Progressive support. The bait in the Speech from the Throne and the hook in the motion which the Minister of Justice endeavoured to move at the opening of the House were the means by which the government tried to land the Progressive support. Does anyone suppose that the Progressive party is going to be entrapped in that way? Every effort has been put forward by the government in order to entrap them. They have been threatened and they have been cajoled, and an insinuation has been made that their indemnities may be lost if the amendment carries, by reason of the fact that the House may dissolve. Everything has been done to enlist their sympathy, and by fair means or foul, to induce them to support the government in the crisis which now faces it. All we ask of the members of the House, all we ask of the Progressive and Independent parties, is that they judge this question on its merits and give it that calm consideration which the Minister of Justice pleaded for. But do not let hon. gentlemen be led astray by these inducements, these blandishments which appear in the Speech from the Throne, ostensibly for the benefit of the Progressive party.
Just a word now in regard to the so-called constitutional question. I realize, as the House does, that this question has already been presented by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) in such a thorough, able and exhaustive manner that little or nothing can be- added to what they have said!. The House is in possession now of all the material precedents and of all the learning that can be got together on the subject; and1 the House will be able to judge. I have only one or two remarks to make upon a single aspect of the constitutional question which by reason arose during the speech of the Solicitor General last night. Now I do not say that I disagree with all the legal argument of my good friend the Solicitor General, for upon many points we are in agreement. He boldly declared that this

Government's Right to Office
parliament had the full right to deal with this question and he laboured his argument very considerably. We all acknowledge his contention on this point on this side of the House; parliament is empowered to deal with the question. The hon. member need not have gone back to the reign of William and M!ary to elaborate a principle which is generally admitted. But the question is, how should parliament deal with the matter? Should parliament deal with it in a legal, constitutional manner, or should parliament consider the matter merely for the purpose of finding a way out for the government from the difficulty which now faces it? I submit that there is only one way to deal with the question, that is, to follow constitutional precedent. If hon. gentlemen will vote in accordance with the law and constitutional precedent governing such a situation they will make no error. My hon. friend said last night that he had been able to find, in the library of this building or somewhere else, precedents which fully sustain the position taken by the Minister of Justice and negative the position taken by the leader of the opposition and the member for West Calgary. And he gave instances.
Before I consider the hon. gentleman's remarks, let me point out that the leader of the Conservative party was very careful indeed to Say that he challenged any man to find a precedent in the last eighty years. There was a reason for his fixing that period of limitation, and the reason was that perhaps the greatest authority on parliamentary usage and custom, the late William Ewart Gladstone, announced in speeches and in written works that our constitution only became firmly established and accepted, So far as cabinet government and ministerial responsibility was concerned, subsequent to the year 1845. That is why my right hon. friend fixed that period of eighty years; it is approximately eighty years since that principle was so fully recognized. Now, in the alleged precedent as cited by the Solicitor General you will note, first, that he has gone far behind the limitation, back to the year 1792, taking the well-known Pitt case, a case which is by no means unknown but which has been discussed in the newspapers of this country recently, and the full details of which were in the possession of the hon. member for West Calgary when he spoke yesterday, but the Pitt case was not referred to by him because he realized that it was not a precedent at all. The Pitt case was a most exceptional case and arose as a matter of fact
many years before our constitutional custom or usage was settled. How did it arise? In 1792 William Pitt was Prime Minister of England and supported by a large majority in parliament. He was appointed to the warden-ship of the Cinque Ports, which is an office carrying emolument, and by reason thereof his seat became vacated. Before the vacation of his seat in the House of Commons he summoned parliament, and parliament was to meet in January following. My hon. friend the Solicitor General shakes his head; we will settle it now; I have the proclamation here. Pitt summoned parliament to meet on January 3 following. Upon vacating his seat he accepted the nomination for the University of Cambridge, and he was elected and returned for that seat on December 17. My hon. friend the Solicitor General gave a very real description of the situation as it existed in England at that time. He said -that it was tlhe time of .the French revolution; all Europe was ablaze; there was tremendous excitement in London, mobs parading the streets, and as a matter of fact historians all refer to these matters. Tht public excitement was great; the regular regiments had been called out; the king himself under his royal sign manual called out the militia, and the Militia Act provided that if the militia were called out at any time, within fourteen days thereafter parliament must be convoked. Parliament had been summoned1 by William Pitt for January 3. But when the king called out the militia parliament had to be convoked within fourteen days, and1 was so convoked-I have here the proclamation calling it-and it met on December 13. That is. the incident my hon. friend referred to.

speechtext:
In fairness to myself I
think my hon. friend will state that the argument I made was that parliament met when the Prime Minister was not a member of either house, which was the case.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
I think technically there
may be something in that, because among the historical writers who advert to this very case one says that four days elapsed before the Prime Minister was returned ,to parliament, another that he was absent for five days, and a third that there is only a tradition to the effect that he -was not in his place in the House. There seems to be no certainty on that point. The records ^how that he was returned when parliament was convoked for a special purpose in a special way, but the date of the precedent is ,all-important, the surroundings and the circumstances are all important, and if conditions existed in Canada,
Government's Right to Office

to-day such as existed in England in 1792 no one would raise a voice in protest over an irregularity such as the absence of the Prime Minister. For these reasons this case has never been cited as a precedent to show that the Prime Minister of the country can be without a seat in either house.
But apart from that, let us take the speeches and .writings of Mr. Gladstone upon the subject. The Pitt case was in 1792. Mr. Gladstone has assured the British speaking world that until after the year 1845 the practice in regard to seats of cabinet ministers was not j settled practice, and the usage was not a well-defined usage. Why go behind that date for precedents? Every precedent from 1845 down to the present day supports the argument- of my right hon. leader and the member for West Calgary that the government cannot function while the Prime Minister is without a seat in either house.

Would my hon. friend

speechtext:
I remember the incident, and I remember that Sir Mackenzie Bowell was a senator of Canada and did resign as Prime Minister of Canada, and (that Sir Charles Tupper came to Canada from England, was elected for a riding in Nova Scotia, and subsequently became Prime Minister. That is as I understand it; if I am wrong in my facts, some one will no doubt correct me, because I have not looked at that particular case recently.
The other case cited by my hon. friend the Solictor General last night was the Baldwin case. That, too, takes us back to 1842, 
and it was the case of the late Robert Baldwin, which arose in the old parliament of United Canada one year after the Act of Union came into force. I have always considered that Robert Baldwin was not Prime Minister in the government of that day. Robert Baldwin -was not called the Prime Minister, and the government is known in history as tihe Lafontaine-Baldwin government. Mr. Lafontaine was elected for Hastings. Mr. Baldwin was defeated in the fourth division of York and afterwards in the second division of A ork, ultimately obtaining a seat in the province of Quebec. There was a dual system of leadership in Canada at that time. It was argued by some then that a government, to be in power, must have a majority in Ontario and a majority in Quebec. Certain it is that they had two prime ministers or leaders in those days, and the fact that Mr. Baldwin was defeated while Mr. Lafontaine, the head of the government, remained in power and in his seat surely can have no bearing, and cannot be quoted as a precedent in this case. Those were the only two precedents that were raised; they are not precedents at all.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext: May I call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that Lafontaine was also elected during the session and for a while, if Lafontaine was Prime Minister, there was no Prime Minister in -the House. They both went to the country at the same time.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
I think perhaps something like that did take place, but the House was adjourned to allow the leaders to find places. During the adjournment Lafontaine was returned, and Baldwin defeated, and the government did not -attempt to function. That is another point. However, if I am wrong in this perhaps some hon. member will correct me. That government is called and known in history as the Lafontaine-Baldwin government. Lafontaine was not defeated; he never lost his seat; there was no vacancy so far as he was concerned. He was Premier and Attorney General for Lower Canada, and Baldwin was Attorney General for Upper Canada; there was a dual system, a dual leadership, and if one leader was in the House and the other out of the House I think the wishes of all parties were satisfied, and the requirements of the law fulfilled.
Now then, what other precedents have been cited? Quotation after quotation has been given from the leading authorities on constitutional law. We need not encumber the record with them. The point is so clear that he who runs may read. A man to be the head of the government, to be the Prime

Government's Right to Office
Minister, under British constitutional law and practice, must have a seat in parliament. My hon. friend stated' the case admirably last night when he said, " I agree to that proposition of law." Then why argue it further? The So'icitor General agrees, we all agTee; but the Solicitor General added as a condition, that it did not matter if the absence was only temporary. Now who can assure this House that the absence of the Prime Minister is only temporary? That is a practical question and no lion, member has the right to speak for the Prime Minister in this House. The Prime Minister is excluded from this House and from, its precincts. He has no right to speak here or to be heard here; he has no more right than has John Smith or Tom Brown walking along the streets of Montreal or Toronto. The Prime Minister is a stranger to this parliament, and although two hon. members yesterday interrupted on behalf of the Prime Minister, they had no right to do so. In one case a member rose to deny a statement made by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to the effect that the Prime Minister speaking in Edmonton had made certain references to the indemnity of the Progressives. The denial would have been very proper had the Prime Minister been here, and had he been in a position to make it, but nobody has the right to do it for him in his absence. He is excluded from this parliament, and nobody can speak for him in this House. In the ether case yesterday when some mild criticism was offered of the Prime Minister, an hon. member across the floor immediately got up and said, "You are criticizing a man who is not in the House and cannot answer." That is the difficulty of the situation. Nobody can assure the House that the Prime Minister will come back. He cannot do so himself. He has been out of the House now for well on to a week, and if he can continue for a week to be chief adviser of the crown without a seat in either house of parliament, why cannot he go on for several weeks? Why cannot he go on for the whole session or the whole life of parliament? If he is right in doing it for a single week, he would be right in continuing to do so for a parliament. The principle is the same. Where does this lead to? It simply means that we are carried back to pre-revolutionary days, to the year 1688, to the days w'hen a king governed by himself, or through his favourites, when such a thing as parliamentary government and ministerial responsibility did not exist. Is that a serious question, or is it otherwise?
That is the broad question which the House is asked to decide by this amendment.
There is a vast distinction between the case of a prime minister and that of any other defeated minister of the government. My submission is that there is! no government of Canada at this moment. When the head of the government goes, the who'e government goes. The Prime Minister is the only minister chosen by the sovereign or by the sovereign's representative. All the other -ministers are chosen by the Prime Minister and their names submitted to His Excellency. An ordinary minister may resign at any moment, and it does not affect the government; the government continues. But the moment the Prime Minister resigns the whole government disappears, and my submission is that the King government- legally disappeared tlie day this House opened. The other ministers in the cabinet are called advisers to the crown only by courtesy. There is only one actual adviser of the crown. His Excellency accepts advice from bis1 Prime Minister on'y. It is true he consults and has the right to consult his other ministers, and does so in practice, but the only adviser of the sovereign or his representative is -the Prime Minister, and to-day if we have no Prime Minister we have no legally constituted adviser. It is true, generally speaking, that all the ministers are advisers of the crown, in the sense that they advise among themselves; there is a joint responsibility among them, hut their advice, whatever it be, goes to His Excellency through the mouth of the Prime Minister.
Now the situation in parliament at this moment is this: We have a body of men assuming that they themselves constitute the government. There is no member of this House who has the right to approach His Excellency -to-day and tender him advice. There is no link to-day between this House and His Majesty's representative, and there should be. These are some of the irregularities which arise from the situation which has developed	through- the unconstitutional
methods of a man who claims to be Prime Minister of Canada.
I have been asked, "What else could Mr. King do?	What should) he have done?"
We know what he should have done. We know that as soon as he had- obtained the election returns in October last and realized that the popular vote was hopelessly against him, as soon as he realized that 133 of his candidates out of 245 had been defeated at the polls and nine of his ministers defeated, he should have done just what other defeated
Government's Right to Office

prime ministers have done, tendered his resignation to His Excellency. But he did not see fit to do that. I am afraid the Prime Minister is rather of the clinging (kind. He certainly desires to cling to office. We can see from his point of view his real objection to resigning at the time when he should have resigned. He may go to a constituency as did Mr. Baldwin and be defeated; it is very probable he will be defeated if he runs in the province of Ontario. I shall not discuss the subject further except to say this: Anyone who wishes to take the political measure of the Solicitor General or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries only needs to read the files of the press during the last election. They must then be convinced that so far as their work in the last election was concerned the campaign was conducted on the old Conscription Act of nine or ten years ago and a Turkish war to take .place five or six hundred years hence.

After Recess

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
Shortly before the House took recess my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) cited another precedent, or alleged precedent, in regard to the question whether a prime minister could hold office as Prime Minister without a seat in the House, and he instanced the case of Sir Charles Tupper and intimated that Sir Charles Tupper -had occupied the office of Prime Minister of this country without a seat in the House. At the time I was unable to look up the citation, but during the adjournment I have been able to do so, and I find that the statement of the Solicitor General in that respect is entirely erroneous. Sir Charles Tupper returned from England to Canada in January, 1S96, and was sworn in as a minister of the crown, with the portfolio of Secretary of State. Immediately thereafter he went down to the riding of Cape Breton for reelection, was returned for that riding and took his seat in the House of Commons as Secretary of State in the Mackenzie Bowell government. That government resigned office on April 27, 1896, when Sir Charles Tupper became Prime Minister, at a time when he certainly occupied a seat in this House as member for the constituency of Cape Breton.
I have now covered the three alleged precedents which have been mentioned on the government side during this debate and I think I can say with a good deal of assurance that none of them has the slightest application to the case before us at the present time, and that the statement of my hon. friend and leader (Mr. Meighen) on Friday last, that you could trace all precedents and all authorities for the last eighty years and you could not find a single instance of a prime minister who had not a seat in one or other of the houses of parliament, either in this country or in- Great Britain, has been verified. No precedent can be found to justify
Government's Right to Office

the Prime Minister of this country in the extraordinary position which he has taken or in his determination to hold on to office.
Passing, however, from -that particular branch of the subject, let me say a few words upon another branch which is, I think, of great importance in the discussion of this subject, and which has not yet been sufficiently emphasized or discussed by this House. We have heard something in the course of this debate of the possible results of whatever action the House may take on this motion. It has been intimated that if this motion carries the government will of necessity resign, and that the country will immediately afterwards be plunged into a general election. It has been intimated, on the other hand, that if this motion is defeated the government will seek an adjournment of the House to enable them to complete their cabinet, and that the House will be reassembled later on and the ordinary work of the session will proceed. I do not know that we are much concerned, or should be much concerned, with the ultimate result in a matter of this kind. We should be more concerned with upholding constitutional authority, be the result what it may. However, I propose to discuss very briefly what may possibly result from the adoption or from the rejection of this motion. Unfortunately we have not the advantage to-night of the presence in this House of the Prime Minister. We can obtain no leadership from him, no guidance from him; but in another view of the question we are fortunate, because we know precisely what he would do, and what he said he would do, under a given set of circumstances which has now arisen in this House. I propose, therefore, to look at the great speech, the preelection pronouncement of the Prime Minister of this country, made upon a formal and solemn occasion, when he informed the electors of Canada, why he had decided to dissolve the House, and what would be done, or what he proposed to do in regard to the future. If the speech which the Prime Minister delivered to his constituents on the 7th September last at Richmond Hill were in the nature of an offhand statement made by a minister on the hustings or on any other similar occasion, I would not take it too seriously. But when the head of a government, at a critical time prior to a genera! election, gives to the Canadian electorate a manifesto or formal pronouncement of his sincere views and conclusions, the people of the country are entitled' to take him at his word.

The last parliament was elected for the usual parliamentary term of five years. It had run but three years and a half at the time the Prime Minister determined upon a dissolution. After the general election of 1921 the government was able to count about one-half of the House of Commons as its supporters. The Conservative party mustered only something like fifty or fifty-two supporters. The remainder of the House, to the extent of some sixty-seven, was madie up of Progressives and Independents. Foir three years the Prime Minister struggled along under what, I admit, were very adverse circumstances. We have seen him and his government humiliated in this House. Those of us who sat in the last parliament will remember many an instance of this kind simply because the Prime Minister was not sufficiently in control of parliament to carry on the government. He must have felt that the humiliation and the experience was a trying one for any government. That the government failed was not wholly its own fault. It was the fault of the composition of the House of Commons which differed from the government to a very great extent. Let us recollect that night when perhaps the most- popular member of the administration was humiliated in this parliament. Those of us who are here will remember *when Mr. Graham, then Minister of National Defence, brought in his militia estimates, assuring the House that he had cut the amount down to the last dollar and saying:	"If I cut them
another dollar, I shall have to go below the margin of safety, which I cannot do." We on this side of the House cheered him. If a minister of national defence has one duty it is to keep up the margin of safety in our national defence. Yet his own followers repudiated him. Chaos arose in the Chamber: the militia estimates had to be withdrawn, and two days later Mr. Graham had to come to parliament and say:	"Notwithstanding
my assurance that I had cut my vote down to the margin of safety, I have had to take some two or three hundred thousand more off and consequently I have gone below the margin of safety." The government could not do otherwise and hold office. That is only one instance. Take the freight rates muddle into which this government plunged the country,

not of their own volition, I grant, but through force of circumstances; because the government was not strong enough in the House of Commons to resist the demands that were made upon them.
Take the lake freights fiasco, where the government, yielding to demands made at

Government's Right to Office
that time, passed laws in this parliament which they could not enforce, and the whole country was humiliated by the fact -that notice had to be given subsequently by the government to American vessel owners that they might disregard Canadian laws. Take the annual tariff tinkering. Take a prime minister who was a member of a government that enacted the FieldingiLaurier -tariff-I supported it in those days and I was proud of it, thinking it was a good ita.riff; a prime minister who was in the government which passed (the 1907 tariff at the demand- of opposing forces in -the House of Commons he had to tinker with it at practically eveiy session until he took all the protective element out of it. He -rendered if innocuous and worthless for any -purpose whatever, not' because -he desired to do so but because he was forced to do so owing to the situation in the House of Commons. I have mentioned only a few of the muddles and a few of the difficulties of the King government during three and a -half years.

speechtext:
I will leave that to somebody else to deal with. These are only a few of the muddles, misfits and miscalculations of the government. We sympathised with the Prime -Minister and his colleagues m his troubles. He was entitled to sympathy. He had a hard load to carry, and after three years and a half-not five years, which was the parliamentary -term-he concluded that things could not continue. He concluded that he had not the support of this House to the extent that he should have it if he was to give a satisfactory account of himself and properly govern the country. He had actually the support of half the House in those days. Now he says, to quote in his own words: "I consulted with my colleagues over the situation." I fancy all the ministers at present sitting in this chamber were consulted upon the situation last September by the Prime Minister and after consultation with his colleagues he prepared for the people of Canada a formal pronouncement, a serious document based on -three and a half years of parliamentary experience, of governing under adverse conditions; a document meant for the electorate of the Dominion of Canada, prepared in advance and circulated amongst the newspapers of Canada in advance. In the town in which I live I was told in the morning of the day on which the speech was delivered that I could see it in the newspaper office. It was a speech -much advertised, much heralded, a speech of which the Toronto Daily Star says: "There was a tremendous crowd to
hear it and over five hundred thousand people heard it by radio." The speech was published in every quarter of the Dominion and it was intended as an official manifesto to the people of Canada. Let us take the Prime Minister at his word-but perhaps I had better put on Hansard his exact language, although it is already there. He said:
As I have already said, I have not the least doubt we shall be able to command such support as we all along have had in the House of Commons at another session; but shall we be able to do more than that? That is the question I have put to every one of my colleagues in the government, and to not a few of the members. It is a question I now put to you who have honoured me with your representation in the House of Commons. It is a question I put to the electorate of this country. Is it sufficient that as a government we should continue in office, drawing our indemnities as members and ministers, and enjoying the other fruits of office, when great national questions press for solution, with which for want of an adequate majority in parliament we are unable satisfactorily to cope ?
Let me read another quotation further on.
I refer now to all important national problems that are pressing for solution, and which cannot be solved in a parliament constituted after the manner of a parliament elected in 1921, or by any government which does not command a substantial majority in the House of Commons.
Further down:
At most we would be reduced to marking time. This is not a moment in our country's affairs at' which to mark time; it is a time to march forward.
Then later on:
May I say further, I believe each of the problems mentioned is a pressing one; I do not believe any one of the four can be dealt with effectively at a last session of parliament. They can only be satisfactorily dealt with by a House of Commons fresh from the people and with a mandate from the people to carry out their will. I would say -further, I do not believe that any one of the four can be dealt with effectively by a government which is not supported by a substantial majority in the House of Commons. Group government and minority government may be inevitable in transitional phases of our political history, but neither is the kind of government wherewith to achieve great reforms.
That, Mr. Speaker, was a solemn official pronouncement and expressed, I believe, the considered judgment, the absolute conviction of the Prime Minister and his colleagues. May I quote in respect of that speech what the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) said last night in reference to the speech alleged to have been made by my leader (Mr. Meighen) in Hamilton? I will use the very words of the Solicitor General and ask the House to apply them to the position of the Prime Minister himself. Speaking last night the Solicitor General said:
Your leader was either sincere when he made his declaration in Hamilton or he was not.
Government's Right to Office

I say to the government: Your leader was either sincere when he made his declaration at Richmond Hill or he was not.
If he was sincere, how many will stand up in this House and support him?
I ask hon. gentlemen opposite now, how many of them will stand up and support what their leader said at Richmond Hill?

I ask the hon. gentleman the same question in regard to his leader's speech at Richmond Hill

from a stupid man?

speechtext:
The hon. member asked further:
If he was not sincere do you think for one moment that he should become Premier of Canada?
I put the same question in regard to the Prime Minister's speech at Richmond Hill. If he was not sincere in that solemn pro? nouncement to the electors of Canada as to his difficulties in the past and his prospects for the future; if that pronouncement was merely a piece of cold calculated deception- which I am sure it was not-he should be rejected not only by the House but by every voter in the Dominion of Canada. Every hon. member of this House knows in his heart that the statement was genuine; it was sincere. The statement was made after the Prime Minister had had a conference with all his colleagues, and it came after an experience of three and a half years of government under adverse circumstances, when he had at his command one half of the House of Commons at least, or a majority of two. as I think he said in his speech. The Prime Minister pictured to the people of Canada four great outstanding problems with which he said he was unable to cope unless he had a substantial majority in the House of Commons. And they were important questions. Transportation was a mighty problem; the

railway problem was another one of tremendous importance; and immigration and senate reform were also both vital questions. These I think were the questions which he was discussing at the time, and his statement was that unless he had a substantial parliamentary majority he could not cope with them and that all he could do for Canada was to mark time or, in other words, to stagnate. This, he said, was a time for marching forward, and without a substantial parliamentary majority it was impossible for him to do so. That is a plain statement; it is a fair, honest, candid statement based upon conviction and experience, and made a few short months ago, seven weeks before the election and two or three days prior to dissolution. Has anyone any doubt as to the reasons he gave His Excellency for obtaining a dissolution? In the very language of his speech you will find his reasons set out.
Now. in a body of serious-minded men such as we find in this House, for the most part business men, what should we do with that statement before us? What is our duty in the matter? Here is a situation far worse, from the Prime Minister's point of view, than anything he ever experienced in the last House. There he had 116 or 117 members while here he has 101. Here the Conservative opposition comprises 116 members while in the last House it numbered only 51 or 52-48, someone says. In the last House the Prime Minister had the support of some 67 Progressives and Independents; in this House the members of these groups number only 28. If his statement was sincere is jt not our duty to take him at his word? Should we not believe him? I will put a question to my hon. friends in the far corner, some of whom have expressed some concern as to what might happen in the event of this amendment either carrying or being rejected. What will any man say to his constituents if he votes to retain this government in power, having before him positive notice from the Prime Minister himself that he cannot do more than mark time, that he cannot cope with the great and pressing questions that confront the Dominion of Canada to-day under existing conditions in this House? Would any man in his right senses employ as manager for his farm or his business or his factory one who said at the outset that under the conditions then existing he could only mark time and could not cope with the big ends of the concern? If such a man should say, "This i3 a time for marching forward but jl can only mark time," would any one of us employ him to manage anything at all? Then, if not

Government's Right to Office
in private or in corporate business, would you ask such a man to manage the affairs of this great Dominion after he had1 solemnly assured the people that he could not cope with the great questions under such conditions as exist at this very moment? If we are honest with ourselves; if we are honest with the Prime Minister himself; if we take his statement as an honest, truthful assertion of his conviction and of his experience, and of what he will do in the future under conditions similar to those which exist in this House today, there is no alternative in regard to our vote on this matter. I submit that no member of this House should look beyond the question in the resolution; but if we are tempted to go beyond it, if we are tempted to consider ulterior results, then let me say this in the presence of my leader and with his authority, that if this motion carries, if this government resigns, and if he is called upon to form a' government in this House, he will undertake the task. He will undertake to carry on that government from session to session without dissolution, and he will do so just so long as he receives parliamentary support. Hon. members who form the Progressive group in this House will realize this: Their position will be just as strong under a new administration as it is under the presejit one. They will occupy the same dominant position in the councils of this House as they do to-day, and if a new government were formed and legislation satisfactory to them introduced and proceeded with, there is no reason why such a government should not continue to the end of the parliamentary term. But the Progressives have this safety valve. Should legislation be introduced not acceptable to them, then on account of the peculiar position which they occupy, they would have the remedy in their own hands. Oh, let no hon. member fear the result of this motion. If this government is displaced a new government will be formed under a leader who is outstanding in the political life of this country, a leader in whose ability we trust, whose courage we know, who is not afraid to cope with those great questions which' demand settlement and which, on his own statement, the present Prime Minister is unable to cope with. How, without repudiating the Prime Minister; how, without telling him to his face, "You did not tell the truth on September 7", a man can vote now against this amendment, I do not know. If the Prime Minister spoke the truth in his speech at Richmond Hill, surely we can take him at his word. If he did not speak the truth to the electors at Richmond Hill, then 14011-7
lie has no right to occupy any position in this House.
Now, Air. Speaker, I sincerely hope that the House may not be led away by any ulterior consideration or by any side issue. I trust that when we come to vote we will vote upon the simple question that is before the House. That, it is true, is a constitutional question, but it has a very large and important practical side to it: Shall we uphold by our votes in this House the constitutional usage and practice of all British parliaments in all quarters of the world?
