What
I have stated is correct, as hon. members will see if they look up the figures. On October 29 there were elected to parliament 116 Conservatives, 101 Liberals, 24 Progressives, 2 Labour, and 2 Independants, tl am interested in what my hon. friend said in this connection just before he sat down, because this is a question which agitated our minds very considerably - not the question. I may say whether my hon. friend would accept the obligation of carrying on government with a minority in this House That was not the point upon which we had doubt: we always felt that he would attempt to carry on government. Perhaps I had better speak for myself in that respect: I had no doubt that he would make the attempt. He would not care to plunge the country into another election, nor indeed would it be wise for him to do so until he had made an attempt to carry on. Therefore, :I personally have no doubts about what he might do, but I do think that some consideration should be given to the situation that we found ourselves in after the 29th of October. We found that the Conservatives had 116 members in this House, the Liberals 101, and the Progressives 24, and an analysis of the vote later on showed-I men-

tion this because my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) raised the question the other day when he was speaking-that the combined vote of Liberals and Progressives resulted in a plurality of 80,000 votes over the votes polled by the Conservatives. My hon. friend from West Calgary argued the other night that because of the adverse vote of the Conservatives and Progressives, we had a right to assume that the whole vote was an adverse vote. I am going to argue, Mr. Speaker, that it was not, and is not an adverse vote to the government of this country.
The Progressives did not and were not claiming that they would have sufficient strength to form a government. They were appealing upon a platform more radical than that of the Liberal party. That has been their programme ever since I have known anything about the formation of that party, and I have no quarrel with their endeavours in that direction. But I say that to assume, as my hon. friend from West Calgary assumed, that the Progressive vote should be counted against the government of the day is hardly fair, and I propose to give reasons why I think my statement is correct.

How about the seventeen
Progressives that ran against Liberal candidates only?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My
hon. friend knows full well that in almost every constituency where a Progressive was up for re-election there was a three-cornered fight.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There
were only two exceptions in Alberta.

And three in British
Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Three who were opposed only by Liberals?
No Liberals running in three constituencies, by arrangement with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
All
the more reason, then, for me to assume that the votes given for the Progressive party were more favourable to the Liberals than to anybody else.
In my question I was referring to Progressives who ran against Liberals and Liberals alone, not against Conservatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look the situation over, he

Government's Right to Office
will find that the preponderance of votes was in favour of the Progressives and Liberals rather than the Progressives and Conservatives. Does my hon. friend know of a single ease, except one, and that was in a constituency in Alberta, in which the Conservative candidate did not offer himself for re-election?

I understand there was
more than one.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not
that I know of. The constituency of Vegre-ville was the only one in our province.

There was no Liberal
candidate in Lethbridge.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No,
because the Liberals and Progressives combined in Lethbridge. All these facts only strengthen my argument. I say that the combined vote of Liberals and Progressives amounted to 80,000 more than the votes polled for the Conservative party.
May I state this, as an added reason why my right hon. friend would not appeal to the country? The character of the campaign waged by the Conservative party against the Prime Minister of this country, against alleged acts of his and otherwise, had the desired effect, of course, in the old province of Ontario, where protectionist feeling ran higher than in any other part of Canada, and the Prime Minister was defeated in that province. He was maligned from every platform wherever it was humanly possible to do so, something that he did not deserve. His services for Canada warranted better treatment than he received at the hands of his opponents in the last election. I make this prediction and throw out this challenge to hoij. gentlemen opposite: Bring on your election if you are successful in this vote, and I predict that there will not be 116 sitting on that side of the House or on this side of the House after any election that may be brought on either by this government or by my right hon, friend should he succeed to the office of Prime Minister of this country.
More than that, Mr. Speaker, while I am on the subject of majorities, I was intensely interested in what my friend the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa.) had to say this afternoon about the great cities of Toronto and Montreal. I would point out to the Toronto members and to the House that the Toronto seats accounted for more than one half of the majority of the Conservatives over that of the Liberals. It seems to me on examining these figures that they must have killed and buried all the Grits in the city of
14011-7J
Toronto. Apparently no Grits li^e there. They may live in the rural parts, but they certainly do not live in the city of Toronto.
That is where Mr. Mackenzie King had lived and was well known, and there was a majority of 100,000 against him.
That is where he got his black eye.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My
hon. friends took care of that. But what was the issue in the last election?
The government.
The Turkish war, in Quebec.
Order. May I ask hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House kindly not to interrupt?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The tariff was the fighting ground in the last election, and that issue was chosen by my right hon. friend. It certainly was the issue in Ontario.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It
certainly was the issue in western Canada, and throughout the whole length and breadth of this country. My hon. friend from Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) will not deny that it was the issue in British Columbia.

The death-knell
of protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friends do not seem to like the remarks L am making.
Order. So far the debate has been kept on a very high plane, and I hope that interruptions from any part of the House will cease.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry if the truths I am trying to propound do not appeal to my hon. friends. I am propounding them in good faith. I say that the issue in the last election was the tariff, and that my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition chose that issue. He wanted to fight the election upon that issue, and he appealed to the electorate upon it.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My
right hon. friend admits that. Therefore, there can be no question about what the electorate passed judgment upon in the last election. There may have been other issues

Government's Right to Office
raised in ''the Maritime provinces. I regret I do not know the situation there as well as I should as a member of the government. Maritime rights seems to have been an issue in those provinces.
The tariff was the issue there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And the tariff? All right. I am quite certain my right hon. friend would make the tariff the issue.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He
made it the issue in our province, and succeeded in wresting one seat at least from us on that issue although he did not get any others. My good friend the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) won his constituency on his own popularity and his reputation. But we accept that issue. I do not want -to stray outside the confines of the discussion of this question. I have not argued on .the constitutional aspect of the matter, I am arguing the situation as it exists now, and this was the situation we had to face. The issue was the tariff. The election was fought upon that question; and when the smoke of battle cleared away my right hon. friend had one hundred and sixteen supporters. I am safe in assuming the issue was as I have stated and we had to recognize the fact in deciding what action we should take in the light of the results on the night of 29th October.

Does the minister suggest that the tariff was the chief issue in the province of Quebec?
Borne hon. MEMBERS: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My
right hon. friend admitted a moment ago that the tariff was the issue from one end of Canada to the other.
Oh no. You asked about the Maritime provinces. I said it was in Ontario and the west, I did not say the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
kept away from Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have heard a great dehl about the province of Quebec and the issues the supporters of my right hon. friend were putting forward there. I want to make it clear that so far as we were concerned the tariff was the issue and the electorate of Canada passed their opinion upon it.
[Mr. C. A. Stewart.l

Does the minister not know
that East Edmonton was not won at all on the tariff, but on the question of the development of the coal industry of Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do
not think my hon. friend would argue that he would have won at all had not the right hon. leader of the opposition come along and proposed putting a duty on coal sufficient to enable Alberta coal to be brought to the central provinces. That and nothing else won East Edmonton, and that was the situation I had reference to when I mentioned the fact before. It w*as the promise of my right hon. friend when speaking in Edimonton, in addition to the other promises lie had made, that he would put on sufficient duty to enable coal to be brought from Alberta and marketed in the central provinces of Canada.
Will the hon. gentleman quote my words please?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I
have not the exact words of my right hon. friend. Will he deny that he made that statement?

I certainly did not use
those words at all. I said with respect to
the coal duties just what I said in the House of Commons on June 2.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry. I am very sorry that the newspapers have the habit of misrepresenting the right hon. gentleman's statements so frequently.

I think they did get
them right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well,
if they did get them right my right hon. friend certainly did not say in the House that he would put on a duty sufficient to bring coal from Alberta to the central provinces of Canada.
Nor did he say it there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of
course I have to accept the right hon. gentleman's word, and I am prepared to do so; but the electors of East Edmonton believed that and voted on that assurance. If the hon. member who represents East Edmonton does not believe that was the promise made to his electors I would like him to say so. That was my understanding.

The hon. gentleman, if
he has read any report whatever on the subject, will know that I said that I would put an increased duty on coal and that I also would provide moneys for the purpose of assisting transportation.

Government's Right to Office

East Edmonton was won not by reason of any statement which the minister credits to the right hon. leader of the opposition but as the result of the general policy of the leader of the opposition to assist the development of the Alberta coal industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I
accept the statement of my hon. friend because he is a man of honour. All I can say is I do not think he, or anyone else, will deny that his success depended very largely upon the statements made in Edmonton upon the occasion referred to.
However, let me go on and develop my argument. I have said, I do not think anyone will deny it, that the election was fought upon the tariff issue and upon that issue only. In that connection I had a number of quotations which I had intended to read. However let me say this in order that I may conclude my remarks in reasonable time: Having considered the situation the Right Hon. Mackenzie King decided to recommend to His Excellency that owing to this peculiar situation that had arisen while, perhaps, we had no right to expect the unanimous support of the Progressive party we did think we could hope for their support in a very large degree, and that the proper thing to do was to refrain for as short a period as possible from making appointments and from the passing of orders in council that might have far reaching consequences-that we would carry on and have His Excellency summon parliament at the earliest possible moment to decide this question. That was the primary reason which influenced us. My right hon. friend has made very many definite pronouncements about the tariff, and he has made some that would have a far-reaching effect. Pie has said on almost every occasion that if he were returned to power he would have an allround increase in the tariff. That has been his statement. I have heard the statement attributed to him-I never heard him make it-that he would raise the tariff as high as that of the United States. WTe all know how high the tariff wall of the United States has been. But let us take his own words, the words I have heard him utter, in favour of an all-round revision of the tariff upwards.
The hon. gentleman has not heard me utter those words either. He cannot find them even in the press.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend deny that he made the statement that he would put up the tariff brick for brick with the United States?

I have told the hon. gentleman a dozen times that I did not. What I stated was-perhaps the hon. member will remember after I tell him now-that as respects farm products I would raise the Canadian tariff to the American level.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know perfectly well my right hon. friend made that statement at Portage but he made it after the election.
He made it after the election and at least fifty times before.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I must accept the corrections of my right hon. friend, but surely he is not going to take the position now that be does not intend to readjust the tariff in accordance with the pre-election promises as to which his supporters have been maligning my right hon. leader-surely not? That being the case, is it not fair to assume, that he took the proper course in remaining in office as adviser of His Excellency until parliament could be convened, and this question submitted to the highest court in the land, that of parliament itself. May I say to my hon. friend and to the members on that side of the House that I for one do not care to remain here and carry on the affairs of this country one moment longer than the moment at which my hon. friends opposite secure a majority vote. When that moment arrives I am prepared to resign, with my leader, and get out.
You could not do any better.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, of course not, but I want to make it clear to hon. gentlemen, because it is very apparent that they do not want to listen to any statement made by members on this side of the House, but rather would assume-and I resent the accusation-tJhat we hang on to office for the fruits of office. What is the other paramount reason?
Does the minister approve of the statements made by the Prime Minister at Richmond Hill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will deal with the statement of the Prime Minister later. I say-and I think the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) will bear me out-that there is another and a very much more important reason, and one that should be given some thought in this House, and that is the situation as it exists to-day in Canada. My right hon. friend has twitted the members from Quebec by making the

Government's Right to Office
statement that the election was not won on the tariff in that province. I am simply using his own remarks. What is the situation that we found after the 29th October? We found that in Ontario over 69 seats had gone Conservative, that in the province of Quebec 61 seats had gone Liberal, and that a situation existed which is not very pleasant to contemplate. Someone remarked, delving into ancient history, dealing with the situation in Europe, 'bat those were strenuous and dangerous days. Liet me say to members of the opposition and to members of the House generally that I consider we are passing through strenuous and dangerous days in Canada. It is important that we should get down to the proper viewpoint. I do not believe, no matter what may be said and no matter how much it may be desired by hon. members of this House, that we will get back ,to the two-party system. We are not going to get back to the two-party system in any great hurry in Canada. We have to face the situation and I think it is important, in a calm and deliberative chamber such as this, that questions of this kind should be given the earnest consideration of members and that with respect to a matter that is so important as the one we are discussing to-night, having in view the desire that peace and harmony shall prevail from one end of the country to the other they should vote in accordance with their judgment. Not so very long before the election I heard statements made by individuals in the Maritime provinces, that unless redress were given to the Mari-times and a fair deal accorded them, drastic action of some sort would be taken. I know the statement has been made in western Canada that unless further relief in the way of tariff and the keeping of contracts with the people were granted some drastic action might be taken in that country. Perhaps those people are not representative, and their advice would not be taken-indeed, I believe it would not be-but at the same time, Mr. Speaker, some attention must be paid to their demands and it is not becoming when a matter of such vital importance as this is being discussed, that we should discuss it heatedly and try to make political capital out of it. It.is well that we should approach it calmly and considerately, having in mind that we are the representatives selected by the people of this country to carry on their business.
The Prime Minister has, up to this moment, acted strictly in a legal capacity. I do not agree with the argument of my hon. friend that because he is unable to take his place in the House the government of the day {Mr. C. A. Stewart.]
cannot function, and I do not believe that we have done anything that is not quite proper. I listened very carefully to thq argument of the hon. member for West Calgary and he did not argue that we had, nor do I believe he would present such an argument. We are here to decide whether or not Mr. King shall continue in office. Mr. King did not believe he would be acting properly in taking advantage of the situation to secure a seat for himself until the Speaker should be elected in this House, and a member of the House should resign in the orderly and constitutional way. There may be differences of opinion about that, and I am not going into those differences. But Mr. King will secure a seat, and he will be in this House as the leader of this government at as early a date as possible.
My hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Guthrie) has held out to hon. gentlemen in that corner of the House, whose votes for the time being, at least, are going to decide this issue, that if this government is defeated they need have no fear that my right hon. friend, who undoubtedly would be called upon to form a government, would carry on. Well, I wonder, and I have wondered how long they would carry on if they attempted to increase the tariff in any particular. However we will leave that to their own good judgment. All I can say to my hon. friends in that comer of the House is this: if statements have been made between themselves and their Liberal opponents that would lead them to believe it was their duty to vote for the amendment to the 'Speech from the Throne, then of course it is their duty to do so. But, on the other hand, it seems to me that the vital issue of this election -was one of tariff. If we are wrong in this assumption, wben this vote is taken we will be put right. If that were the vital issue upon which the election was carried on, then it seems to me the programme which of necessity we had to bring down before parliament could be convened might appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite. If it does not appeal to them I have nothing further to say.
At all events, Mr. Speaker, so far we have carried on, we have presented to the House our programme and we have not asked the House to deal with that programme. We are content to abide by the decision upon the point raised by my hon. friend in his amendment, and if the decision is in his favour then of course he will prepare a programme and will carry on. We have not attempted in any particular to usurp any function, and we do not want to remain in office one moment longer than the moment at which a decision can be reached on this question. If we are

Government's Right to Office
sustained, then, I can say to hon. members of this House that we will do our level best to carry out that programme. We will 'try to give the same kind of government in the next two or three years that we have given in the past .
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Some hon.
members seem to think there is something wrong with that. Well the country seems to succeed very well under it. That is one of the sore points with my hon1. friend. Oh, prosperity that was just around the comer came on the jump this fall, and the condition of affairs does not look so gloomy now as it did in 1923. There is a very great change.
Mr. CLARK. There are the crops.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But
if my hon. friends had been in office the crops would not have had anything to do with it; it would have been the change of government that put Canada where she is to-day. Surely my hon. friends will not deny the government some credit for the reductions on basic commodities, which have resulted in such mighty strides; which have increased our exports to the splendid position they stand to-day. Surely the government had something to do with that. But had the government of my right hon. friend come into office on October 29,1 can imagine what would have appeared in the Montreal Gazette, the Mail and Empire, and the Toronto Telegram-splashing front page announcements that because of the change of government this prosperity had come to Canada! But it has arrived with my hon. friends not ip office, and it is going to stay whether they get into office or not.

Prophesying
again.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, it is with us, and the hon. member for Lincoln or any other hon. gentlemen dare not deny it because the facts speak for themselves. That is the situation in Canada.
May I say this to my hon. friends who sit in that corner of the House? Do not be misled by statements of the character of those just made by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I do not ask you to vote for this government. Use your own judgment. We .shall be content to accept the decision of parliament, and speaking personally, I might have a very much easier time should that decision be an adverse one. Any hon. gentleman who has occupied the treasury benches will agree with
me in that. If those who are so anxious to get into office imagine they would be taking over any sinecure in handling one of the departments of the federal government, they would change their minds before they had six months' experience of it,
The hon. member is trying hard to keep it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes,
and I propose to stay. I think I have made some success of the department over which I have control and I am not ashamed of the record of that department.
Is that the Immigration department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the Immigration department, but I will not deal with that now. I hope to be able to deal with that matter on a future occasion, and I shall then be glad to tell my hon. friend all about it. It is not a question which comes up for discussion at this moment. The question we are to ask ourselves now is whether or not, in the light of the issue upon which this election was held, this government did the proper thing in remaining in office and in calling parliament. This government took all the necessary constitutional steps in order to do that, and did it at the earliest possible moment. From the 29th of October onwards this government refrained from taking any advantage that would arise from the making of appointments and otherwise. We have acted conscientiously within the limit of the law, and we are prepared to stand or fall by the decision which will be recorded in this House when the vote is taken.

Mr. Speaker, whatever the present session could possibly contain in the way of disappointments to any members of the House, there is one thing at least in which the fullest of our expectations have been realized already and that is 'that the sitting would contain from the start some very strange and untoward features. For my part, nothing could have appeared stranger to me, sitting in this House as a Canadian of Irish descent, than to hear this afternoon an impassioned appeal by a French-Canadian Nationalist to the parliament of Canada to stand up for the British spirit. It was, perhaps, one of the most gratifying things that a man could have an opportunity of hearing from sudh a source. There are, however, other statements to which I have listened which are not so encouraging. Since the inception of the present debate we have heard the leader of the House, the Minister

Government's Bight to Office
of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) disagree, both in words and in acts, with the declarations of his leader, the former Prime Minister. We have heard the hon. gentleman skate with great skill around and frequently away from the topic that is at present under debate. We heard next the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) adjure this House to adhere to that very topic, and then we heard the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) state openly that he did not propose to discuss it, whereupon he proceeded to discuss everything else m the heavens above, the earth beneath and the waters under the earth. The exceptional and! extraordinary features that began in that way did not even end there. After the Solicitor General had contradicted to a very great extent his leader in the House and his former leader, we heard him proceed finally to contradict himself, and as if not satisfied with that, we heard the hon. gentleman go still further, for yesterday he set out to give us new lessons in theology. When he rose to his feet he told the House that Jericho fell by noise. If my education has not been sadly neglected, Jericho fell by the will of the Lord of Hosts, and if I may remind the hon. gentleman of a fact which, I think, is fairly generally accepted, those who did not profit particularly well afterwards were those who refused to give God the glory. I have been in this House for only three days, but may I say at the outset that in that time I have conceived an extraordinary attachment for hon. gentlemen opposite, and anything I am about to say will be said without any animosity whatever and in the veiy kindest spirit that I can possibly hope to exhibit.
There is but one plain issue before the House at this time, and that is the amendment which my honoured leader has proposed. I- am not going to weary the House by referring to it again excepting to say this, that it has been made the only point under discussion and that, after recitals, it sets out this plain proposition:
That those who now' assume to be His Excellency's advisers are not competent to act as, or to become, the committee of parliament, commonly known as the government.
If that does not restrict the situation to the acts or omissions of our friends opposite,
I cannot imagine what would. There is in this House only one body assuming to be the government, only one body that has had the reins of government for the past three and a half to four years. There is only one body in this House that brought about the recent elections and precipitated the present situation. Now, in addition to the numerical diffi-
culties that confront hon. gentlemen opposite who are seeking to carry on this government, I say that they are indissolubly bound up with their record of achievement or lack of achievement during the past few years. 1 do not desire to weary the House with repetitions of what we have already heard, but I would remind hon. members of the fact that the Prime Minister in his Richmond Hill speech made use of perhaps the most significant expression that he could very well have uttered when he said that "great national issues are pressing for solution." I would invite the leader of the House (Mr. Lapointe) or any other hon. gentleman opposite to inform this House now in what particular sense the pressure to which the Prime Minister referred at that time has in in any way lessened or relaxed.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) stated an undeniable fact, which apparently is recognized by gentlemen on all sides of the House, when he declared that this is a defeated government, and notwithstanding the great amount of juggling that has been attempted with the figures that followed the election I do not think that this fact can at all be concealed from the country. The last speaker, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, West Edmonton), has assured us that prosperity has returned to this land. I wish I had an opportunity to take the hon. gont'eman over to the Niagara frontier and show him the unhappy exodus, which not only has been going on during the last three years but is still going on, of our Canadian citizens. I wonder on what assumption the hon. gentleman bases his claim that there has been a return of prosperity to Canada, when from the city alone which I represent, something like 5,000 of our young men have during the past year gone to the other side to get their daily bread. And this number is small when we realize that the total of those who have been forced to leave the country as a whole within the last three and a half years for the same reason has approximated nearly half a million people. The position, too, is exactly the same in the matter of rural credits, as the hon. member for Kindersley pointed out. During the last three and a half or four years there has been a crying need in this regard, but no action has been taken to better conditions'. There may be a difference of opinion as to how that result could be brought about, but there can be no difference of opinion as to the need itself. That is why I was particularly impressed, in listening to the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite, with the statement that there was a

Government's Right to Office
return of prosperity and that good times were, as they put it, just around the corner.
The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) complained last night, and rightly complained, about the failure to debate the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne before taking up this amendment to the motion of confidence. May I remind him that the reason for this is the very obvious one that the acting government was simply attempting to secure a snap vote of confidence before the Address could be reached. The people of this country, if I have any means of knowing their present temper at all, are not looking for sharp votes or snap judgments or anything of the sort; they simply want an honest and straightforward adjudication upon the merits of the case as between the two old parties and the third party that sits at our left. The proposed motion which was presented to the House by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), it has been suggested by certain members, was rigged up after our leader (Mr. Meighen) hud shown him what his own motion was to be.. I do not believe that; not only is it unfair to the Minister of Justice, but it does not correctly represent the position of either himself or his party. It seems to me that the obvious thing was that this government, or this remnant of a government, wanted to avoid if possible any debate on the Address and so took that means of trying to get a decision upon an entirely irrelevant motion of confidence in itself. It has been'well pointed out that the great feature of the Address is an evident and complete change of heart on the part of the government that offered it, and as a matter of fact the hon. member for Kindersley enumerated in detail yesterday the various directions in which that change is apparent. Not only the members of this House but the country as well will remember that the Prime Minister in the last three and a half years has always declared his intention of effecting great reforms for the purpose of remedying the various ills from which this Dominion has been suffering. But he has consistently given, as two great obstacles to this objective, the obstruction of the Senate and the influence of the Progressive party. He made the statement from many a platform that upon his return to parliament one of the first things he would undertake would be Senate reform of such character that the upper house would be no longer in a position to render legislation futile. And speaking in London on October 16 last he made a statement which, if it is not known to every member of the House and to every man and woman in the country, ought certainly to be very
well known. In the hockey arena in that city on the date I mentioned he said:
Only a few days ago a number of senators were appointed. Every one has given me his pledged word he will be prepared, once a measure passes the Commons, to give it his support. Subsequent senators will be appointed with that understanding, and as Providence takes away a few of the older members, you will have a Senate pledged to bring about the reforms for which the administration stands.
Could a man declare in plainer terms that lie aspired, and was determined to be, a dictator in this country? But even dictators at times experience a change of heart, and perusal of the Speech from the Throne shows that any reference to Senate reform is strangely absent from that document. I could not help wondering whether perhaps a siight reason for that omission was to be found in the fact that the Senate might afford a haven of refuge to that gentleman by the time the House opened the other day. It seemed to me that there might be a very good reason why the raging lion of last year should have become the dove of the present occasion, and I could not help thinking that the ex-Prime Minister's situation might best be described in the well known words:
Like the wandering dove that found No repose on earth around,
He could to that ark repair And enjoy himself but there.
But, Sir, knowing the gentlemans previous attitude, knowing his previous actions, is it not fair to suspect that there may be another change of heart just around the corner, and that should the gentleman be returned to power the dictatorship will again be very much to the fore?
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that we can complain particularly about the attitude of our Liberal friends in one respect. Naturally they desire to cling to what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has described as "the fruits and sweets of office". I do not think we can complain particularly if they adopt the attitude of self-preservation, which they appear to have adopted. Who of us in the golden days of his youth has not seen a decapitated chicken feebly flapping its wings long after its head and body had parted company? I have no objection to any effort on the part of the shattered remnant of the Liberal government to convince itself that its wings still will flap; I have no objection particularly to its attempts at self-deception, but I do object most strenuously to its efforts to deceive parliament, and to deceive the country.

I do not propose to weary the House by any repetition of them at this time, but I submit that precedents, no matter how many you may get, no matter what their particular nature may be, are valuable only as they embody or illustrate great principles. The hon. Minister of Justice took as his starting point the retirement of Disraeli in 1868 after the general election in that year, and if the minister had been so minded he could have gone on and given to the House the expression of principle upon which Mr. Disraeli relied when he voluntarily relinquished office. Mr. Disraeli said on that occasion:
This course was taken because it was due to our own honour, to the personal convenience of the sovereign, and to the progress of public business.
May I ask, Sir, what prospect there can be for the progress of public business if our friends opposite manage in some way to retain power in this House?
Then two precedents were cited by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), and he laid great stress on them; in fact they constituted almost his entire argument. The hon. gentleman said this:
The Salisbury administration in 1886, assuming office on July 26 of that year, had not resigned although it had not succeeded in its next election in getting a majority of the members returned to the House.
Well, that is true, but once again there is an explanation which is vital to a proper understanding. In that election there were returned: Conservatives, 268, Liberal-Unionists, [DOT]17, Gladstone Liberals, 273, and Nationalists, 81. That left the Conservatives in a minority, but the Nationalists having assisted Salisbury in 1885 he had no intimation, until he met the House, that they were not going to be behind him again, which would have given him a very large majority. The only other case cited as a precedent by the Minister of National Defence had to do with the Russell administration in 1816. and there he commented forcibly upon the fact that the ministry had carried on from 1846 until the end of the parliamentary term in 1847. But, in making that comment he omitted to say that the ministry was carried on at the request of the sovereign; that it was carried on with the consent and approbation of the majority of the opposition, and that it was considered to be for the good of the country, and was so expressed by the leader of the opposition.

I would like to know how far we can trust to the sincerity of those who tell this House that everything has been done to put him back at the earliest possible moment, and whether we can be sure that an honest and sincere effort will be made to bring him back as soon as possible. As I listened to the eloquent argument which that gentleman advanced along those lines I could not help thinking what a grievous pity it was that that same great gift of prophecy was not employed by him for the benefit of Mr. Mackenzie King before the election.

that the fact that over 200,000 more Conservative votes were cast in the last election than Liberal votes was not a matter of any particular consequence. He laid stress on the argument, as did the other ministers who followed him, that the deciding factor in the present instance was the supremacy of parliament. The Minister of Justice emphasized that point very strongly. He kept right at it throughout his speech. Why, he asked, should the leader of the opposition desire to become the Prime Minister of Canada if parliament will not let him? I am content, he said, to let parliament rule, having advised the summoning of parliament for the purpose of deciding the issue as to who should constitute the government. I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that the best and most positive answer to the learned gentleman's view has been expressed in this House by the ex-Prime Minister, Mr. King himself. The Minister of Justice professes to consider that parliament is so supreme that the vote of the people is of no consequence, but this is what the exPrime Minister stated to this House on the loth of February, 1921:
Unless we have a representative parliament, what becomes of any theory of the supremacy of parliament? The supremacy of parliament is based in every particular upon the circumstance that parliament is supposed to be truly representative of the will of the people.
And yet the Minister of Justice attempts to convince this parliament that the will of the people is of no account, that parliament can make itself supreme in this matter. I ask, Sir, if on the 15th of February, 1921, when the then Prime Minister made that pronouncement in this House, the Minister of Justice agreed with him? Miss AGNES C. MacPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Mr. Speaker, the hon. members of this new parliament are very kind indeed. However, before addressing a few words to the consideration of the question before the House I want to say that this new parliament 'has been a disappointment to me; it is not anything like so comfortable and agreeable as the one which passed out of existence last

Government's Right to Office
fall; But here it is, and I suppose we will have to do the best we can with it.
This peculiar situation of no party having a majority arose because numbers of people in the country came to the conclusion that each of the historic parties was but a cloak under which powerful economic groups governed. And having tried one and the other they decided that some other method of having their economic interest represented in this House must be found. It is true that in theory the historic parties are not the same. In practice, however, they are, and so after trying first one and then the other, large numbers of people in the constituencies decided that they would send to represent them in the House of Commons people who had- their own economic outlook. Accordingly three new groups found their way into this House-the Farmers group, the Labour and the Independent groups. The two party system under which public administration has been carried on in the past in Canada does not allow these several groups an opportunity to function in the government. The government or the cabinet is not a committee of parliament, as is said in the amendment; it is a committee of the party in power. In practice this committee is not responsible to parliament but controls it because of the slavish following of the usage that the defeat of a ministerial measure means the defeat of the government and a general election.
We have now in this House all the factors needed to form a cabinet which should be responsible to parliament, except the will to try. It is true that such a plan would call for the discarding, first, of the theory of the solidarity of the cabinet-I rather suspect it is mostly theory; and second, of the practice that the defeat of a ministerial measure means the defeat of the government. If in future years groups continue to come to this House, some form of government through which they can function will be found. That is my opinion of whait the British constitution means. It is something that we change as the need arises. And when the need for change works its way into the minds of all the groups in this House and the people in the country, a change that will make for better government than we have at present will be adopted. At present the governing party reminds me of the Irishman who was willing to live not only his own life but the lives of everyone around him. That, I suppose, is why each of the historic parties is striving so strenuously to be the governing group.
Now, regarding the constitutionality of the action of the government in retaining power,
I doubt very much if anyone in this House is qualified to give an unbiased opinion on the matter. Able lawyers have expressed their views, but could not these hon. members have argued as ably if they had found themselves on the other side of the question and the other side of the House? I think they could. But if hon. gentlemen in this House cannot agree as to the constitutionality of the government's action I believe all can agree that the King government^ played atrociously poor politics when it continued to hold office after the verdict of the people had been given. The effect of this verdict, as I am sure all Liberals will in their hearts but not with their lips admit, is the increasing resentment of the people of Canada against them.
The difficulty for me and for those who are situated as I am in regard to the amendment offered by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is that while it deals solely with the constitutional aspect, the people in the country, possibly because of the press, possibly because they do not understand technicalities-I do not know whether anybody else understands them or not-will look upon this as a vote of confidence or of want of confidence. In fact the papers are now carrying headlines that it is a confidence or a non-confidence motion. During the last parliament the King government gave us only crumbs of reform, and those grudgingly. The King government could have put through any reform which we favoured, but instead of that they chose of their own free will to mark time and to appeal to the country on the plea that they had not a sufficient majority, and now weakened in numbers and in prestige the same government comes back and promises everything. I did not notice about the Christmas turkey. Possibly it is in there too. The Prime Minister during the late campaign made public utterances in regard to the support given him by the Progressive group in the last parliament that showed, to my mind, an utter lack both of gratitude and of graciousness. I want to say quite plainly that I have absolutely no confidence in the King government. I am not pleased1 with their past performances, nor have I faith in their promises of future action. That does not mean that I have not a very great affection for the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) however, but on the other hand, I am not in accord with Conservative policy, nor in sympathy with their mental outlook, and I view with alarm-those seem to me like familiar words-the return of the old war horses of the Conservative party to

the front benches. I do not believe in the election methods of either political party, but in Ontario the method of the Conservative party in financing and conducting elections is particularly disagreeable and does much to lower the tone of public life in Canada. The situation we are attempting to deal with tonight is puzzling, indeed almost mystifying to the ordinary layman, and when the learned jurists on each side of the House disagree, as they have done for the last two days, it would be of course impertinence for a layman like myself to give an opinion on the constitutional aspect of the question. I am not sure whether the King government acted constitutionally when they retained office after the election. Indeed, I am not very greatly concerned, because when parliament opened I know that if parliament did not want that government it could easily have rejected it. I am not going to be very dogmatic about it, because I believe in the will of parliament, not in government. The trouble is that in the past we have had governing groups that dominated parliament. I want to see a parliament that will dominate the groups.
At the opening of parliament the government brought down a resolution demanding a vote of confidence from the House. That resolution was challenged on a point of order. The Speaker has deferred his ruling on that point. Then following that the government introduced another resolution, and to this resolution the right hon. leader of the official opposition moved an amendment. Now, as I see it, the government, in asking for a vote of confidence, says to the group in this section of the House "We are not prepared to cariy on government under these chaotic and precarious conditions, we are not prepared to permit you gentlemen to sit back and judge each piece of legislation on its merits. We may, of course, be sustained to-day and may be defeated to-morrow. In other words, we do not think it advisable to go to the expense of having these by-elections, getting ready for the session of parliament, knowing that we may be defeated at any moment. We have asked you now to [Miss MacPhail.J
define your position, and we ask you to state now whether you can guarantee us a continuity of support through the lifetime of the parliament, in consideration of the attractive promises we have made you in the Speech from the Throne." That, in effect, is the position of the government. I have not any fault to find with their position. I believe with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that an executive could be or ought to be chosen from the floor of the House.
However, we are dealing to-day not with an abstract .theory, but with concrete facts. We are faced -with this situation; there are two traditional parties here who are not prepared to accept this proposition and we in this section of the House, small in number, cannot hope by any stretch of the imagination, to have the whole House accept our view; therefore we are faced with this concrete fact as I understand it-and if I am wrong I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will set me right- that in effect the amendment we are debating is really a vote of confidence and is not actually deciding on the constitutional aspects of the question at all. Therefore it resolves itself into a decision on our part as to whether or not we have confidence in the present government. I think I am right in that. The question for the group in this section of the House to decide is not whether the government's action was constitutional or not, but whether or not, in view of the promises they have made in the Speech from the Throne we are justified in assuring that government a continuity of support for the lifetime of parliament.
How does the hon gentleman consider that we can possibly be discussing the policy of the government, when the Speech from the Throne is not really before us?

That is all we have been discussing these two or three days, the policy of the government, and the latitude permitted to members by His Honour the Speaker in that regard proves to me, if nothing else does, that what we are really dehating is the question of confidence or no confidence in the government.
I am dealing with the problem from that standpoint. I have no criticism to offer of the government for demanding a vote of confidence.
I think if I were on the treasury benches today under such circumstances I would certainly make a similar demand, or refuse to undertake the responsibility of conducting the affairs of the country. Therefore, I say the question resolves itself, so far as we are concerned, into

At the opening of the session of 1924 the Speech from the Throne contained this paragraph:
Among amendments to be proposed to the Dominion Elections Act will be one providing for the use of the transferable' vote in single member constituencies.
This was a clear, definite promise on the part of the government to give us the transferable vote during the 1924 session. A little later on in the session the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) drew the attention of the Prime Minister to an item appearing in the daily press, intimating that the government had no intention of bringing down this piece of legislation. In answer to his question the Prime Minister used these words:
Any intimation that the government has decided that this measure will not be proceeded with is wholly inaccurate.
Those words are also very definite, very Clear cut. There is only one way in which that can be understood, and yet during the session of 1924 nothing whatever -was done to implement that promise. Later on, the hon. member for Brandon again asked a question of the Prime Minister and this is his reply:
I am afraid that if the transferable vote were introduced it might lead to protracted discussion extending over some little time. Under the circumstances, the government has decided not to proceed further with the bill which is before the House at the present time, but to take it up at an early stage at the next session of parliament.
We come to the session of 1925. I find on February 19, 1925, the former hon. member for Brant put a question to the Prime Minister with regard to the same alternative vote. The Prime Minister's answer was very evasive, very cryptic, in fact. He simply told the former hon. member for Brant to "wait and
see." This was a distinct change of front on the part of the Prime Minister. A little later, on March 17, the former hon. member for Marquette put a similar question to the Prime Minister. These were the Prime Ministers words:
The government has not yet definitely decided whether to reintroduce the legislation this session.
Another entire change of front. The former hon. member for Brant said:

The Prime Minister replied:
If I made any such promise it will be carried out and the bill will be brought in.

situation, the more I am coming to the conclusion that such a system simply perpetuates this class group of which I have spoken and which I think is doing more harm to Canada than anything else.
Not very complimentary language addressed to my hon. friends in this section of the House. I am sure if the Prime Minister were here this evening he would use more honeyed words than those. I am quite sure that many thousands of people in the country will agree with the Prime Minister that the Progressive group will be doing more harm to the country than anything else if they keep this government in power.- Yet, again, the Speech from the Throne, delivered a few days ago, intimates that there will be further amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, and I presume this is another promise with regard to the single transferable vote.
I have no intention of laying all the sins of omission and commission on the Prime Minister. I have a very high regard for the present Prime Minister. I believe he is a man with a very broad outlook, a very liberal-minded man at heart, and his party must share a good deal of that responsibility. It is the reactionary influences that have seeped into the Liberal party during the last few years and have sterilized its action, that have been responsible for the position in which the party is to-day, and not alone the action of the Prime Minister, although I believe some Liberals would, perhaps, try to make him the goat and heap all those sins on his shoulders. The Liberal party itself has failed to live up to its great traditions, to uphold the ideals of its own leader, and sometimes, I think, in the most charitable manner-and I have a great regard for some of my Liberal friends-a little period in the wilderness with the purifying influence that would have, would be the very best thing for the great Liberal party. I have a very high regard for that party. I followed! it myself for many years. There were some of us in the west who found at last it was not moving fast enough and we had to step out and go ahead 
a little bit. But I have always hoped and I have never hoped more than I do to-night that the day will come when that party will again raise up its old standard and stand by it and come back to this House what it used to be and what it ought to be, the great protagonist of the great mass of the common people of Canada.
Does the hon. member expect that from the Conservative party?

If my hon. friends will
remain in the cold shades of opposition for a while it will have that purifying effect on them. Let me say that hon. members in this section are called upon to make a decision which is by no means a very pleasant one, and I can assure the House that the position we have reached has not been considered in any partisan spirit. Moreover, it has meant to us many anxious hours and sleepless nights. We in this part of the House do not try to influence any hon. member in the way he should vote, for we believe that it is the duty of every representative of the people in parliament to exercise his own judgment according to the dictates of his conscience. I trust therefore that the decision when it is given, whatever it may be, will be taken in the right spirit. If there is one thing more than another that we in this corner have tried to avoid it is partisan bias, and I do hope that when the vote is taken upon this question hon. gentlemen on all sides of the House will endeavour to forget a little of the party spirit and get down more closely to the management of the country's business. I am sure that all of us, whether we be Liberals or Conservatives, Progressives or Labour or Independent, are anxious to discharge our duty as true Canadian citizens and that we all have the good of the country at heart. Let us therefore all get together to do the best we can in the interests of this great nation.
On motion of Mr. Power the debate was adjourned.

Government's Right to Office

As it is probable that new members of the House are unaware of the fact,
I may state for their information that under the rules the House, in the absence of a special motion to the contrary, meets on Wednesday at two o'clock in the- afternoon. During the past two or three sessions, however, it has been found by common consent more convenient to meet instead at three o'clock and the rule in this respect has therefore been suspended. It is also a rule that the House on Wednesday shall adjourn at six o'clock. The Minister of Justice, in keeping with the recent custom to which I have just referred, moves that the House, when it adjourns now, shall stand adjourned until to-morrow at three o'clock. This motion may be put without previous notice by unanimous consent of the House.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.27 p.m.
